Entertainment.title: How Did A Secretlab Chair End Up in Every Room That Matters?
Entertainment.text: Once you notice it, you can't stop noticing it. It's behind Magnus Carlsen as he dismantles an opponent from home. It's under Hans Zimmer while he builds the low, seismic dread of Dune. It's the seat Keith Gill — Roaring Kitty to the internet — chose to sit on, in its Game of Thrones House Lannister trim, as he faced the US House Financial Services Committee. Jose Mourinho plots in one; Kevin De Bruyne recovers in one; Post Malone, Marshmello, iShowSpeed and Max Verstappen have all shown up in the same tall-backed silhouette.A quick search for "gaming chair" pulls up dozens of near-identical products, which is exactly what makes the real question interesting. It isn't why gaming chairs are having a moment, but more of why this one keeps appearing in rooms that have nothing to do with each other.  View this post on Instagram A post shared by Verstappen Sim Racing (@verstappensimracing)To find out, I flew to Singapore, where Secretlab was founded in 2014 by two former StarCraft II semi-pros, Ian Ang and Alaric Choo. They were training in chairs they couldn't stand, so they decided to build their own.The problem they were solving was specific and punishing. Competitive players can stay seated for up to 16 hours in a single training day. They swing between locked-in concentration and short breaks, and a chair built for that has to stay supportive through all of it, day after day. That spec made the chair a fixture at major esports tournaments, where pros compete for multi-million-dollar prize pools, and in the backgrounds of streamers broadcasting to millions from their bedrooms. Before most people knew the name, they'd already seen the silhouette.The logic that followed was simple: a chair that could keep up with a pro player could keep up with anyone who spends serious time sitting down. The pandemic put that to the test at scale. When work, school and much of social life moved home, millions of people suddenly found themselves at a desk all day and started paying attention to how they felt at the end of it. Plenty of them went looking for the chair that people who never get up were already sitting on. Today, a Secretlab sits in the homes of more than three million people worldwide.That explains how the chair got into all those rooms, but it doesn't explain why it stayed long after the rush to furnish home offices faded, or why an Academy Award-winning composer, a chess grandmaster and a Premier League star would all decide on the same one. For that, you have to go inside.Secretlab's headquarters doesn't perform the way tech offices usually do, and the rooms where the chairs are actually made normally stay shut. Fittingly, the "Secret" in "Secretlab" became the running joke of the day but we got a glimpse of this restricted area. What's immediately evident, though, is the obsession with making everything just a little better each time. The company houses a full materials lab that is anything but quiet. Fabric swatches are pulled taut and released by machines that never tire. Mechanical rigs lower themselves onto seat cushions and lift off again, hundreds of thousands of times over, standing in for a lifetime of people sitting down. The sides of a MAGNUS desk are punched repeatedly to test its balance while, a few feet away, desks are buried under roughly 120 kilograms of steel plates and subjected to accelerated stress tests. I spent the day with designers who talk fluently about the parts of a chair you'll never consciously register: the way a lever feels under the fingers, how pressure is distributed across a seat, or how foam behaves not on day one but after years of daily use.Everything begins with that foam. Secretlab's patent-pending cold-cure formulation is the base of every chair, and the team distinguishes obsessively between immediate comfort and long-term comfort. There's the plush cushion that flatters you in a showroom, and then there's Secretlab's medium-firm support that keeps you productive at hour 12.Foam is also where Secretlab breaks with a good chunk of the traditional ergonomics establishment. Most ergonomic task chairs, the prestige office names like Herman Miller and Steelcase included, are built on breathable mesh, long assumed to be the more supportive material. Newer research complicates that, with a study from the University of California, Berkeley finding no significant difference between mesh and well-engineered foam across key measures of comfort, pain and fatigue. In fact, foam was found to have an edge on pressure distribution and relief. Foam also came out noticeably more supportive over long stretches, which is the whole ballgame for anyone who spends their day in a chair.But not all foam is created equal and Secretlab has certainly gone above and beyond, testing different compositions and baking it in different temperatures till they got the most optimal formulation. In the showroom, they make the case physically: a block of their cold-cure foam sits beside two generic foams, each pinned under a 20-kilogram weight. The two generics had already begun to sag when we broke for lunch, and by the time we came back some two hours later, they'd sunk further still, while the cold-cure block sat exactly as it had that morning. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Secretlab (@secretlab) A lot of what they told me kept coming back to the body. The femur, as they pointed out, is the bone that changes most as a person grows, and which is part of why one chair has to fit such different builds. In the same breath, the lumbar support isn't a firm piece with padding laid over it. The foam is actually moulded over the support structure, which is the reverse of how it's usually done.It makes for slow work — every design goes through rounds of user testing and expert validation. They've got their own independent Ergonomics Advisory Board that works with the engineers on product development reviews. Both their TITAN Evo and ATLAS carry certification from the United States Ergonomics. And nothing ships unless it clears a bar the founders set deliberately high. There have even been instances when a product was so close to production but had to be sent back for final tweaks. "We want the first chair to be the same as the millionth chair," Choo affirmed. I asked whether that ever felt like a drag on progress. He said time wasn't the enemy."We want the first chair to be the same as the millionth chair."Nowhere is that thinking more legible than in the ATLAS, Secretlab's first task chair and the clearest signal of where the company is headed. It is the company's move out of the bedroom and the gaming den and into everyday life. The ATLAS is more understated, and reads just as well in a home office, a study, or a living room as it does at a corporate desk.Where the flagship TITAN Evo — designed to be incredibly versatile — reclines like a lockable bed, the ATLAS is built for the working day. The colors are quieter than you'd expect from a gaming brand, too. There's a new shade called "Dune" alongside the other neutrals, muted enough to sit in an ordinary living room without drawing attention. As Vincent Sin, the brand's Head of Industrial Design, puts it, it's a sign that Secretlab's colorways are maturing along with the company.I sat on both the TITAN Evo and the ATLAS, and what stayed with me was the range each one holds. Drop into the TITAN Evo and you can genuinely slump and drift, the backrest tipping back like a bed; sit up and lock it and your spine lengthens, and you're suddenly locked in yourself. The ATLAS does the same trick in a tighter register, its synchronous tilt loosening for a break and snapping taut for focus. Same object, two completely different use cases, two completely different looks.That range of movement is a subtle but important thing that makes these chairs work across such different lives. Most of us work and chill at the same desk, usually within the same hour, sliding from deep focus to a scroll to a slump and back. A chair that moves with you is less exhausting to sit in all day than one that fights you into a single position. The chair is never the one who decides whether the next few hours are play or labor, and that handover of control to the user is rarer, and more valuable, than it sounds.The ATLAS also shares with the TITAN Evo what Secretlab bills as the world's first magnetized head pillow, which slots into place without a single strap. They deliberately made sure that if you rest your head against it, you can't feel the hardware that holds the pillow in place. It's the kind of detail most people will never consciously notice, and exactly the kind Secretlab keeps sweating anyway. That is, in the end, what sets the brand apart.There's a quiet business logic to that, and it cuts against the industry grain. Most furniture makers would rather sell you a whole new chair, but Secretlab has built an upgrade ecosystem around the one you already own. An OTTO Adjustable Legrest props your feet up, an Ergonomic Recliner Add-On turns an upright chair into something you can lie back in, and the new Easyfold Foldaway Armrests give you extra horizontal room. They all go on and come off in minutes. That intuitive, no-instructions fit is a point of principle for Ang, who thinks a user should be able to set one up straight out of the box. "A good product should be something you can use easily," Ang says, reflecting the brand's design language. People rarely know what to ask for, the team told me, and Secretlab's job is to make the right call for them, then prove it."A good product should be something you can use easily."Crucially, these add-ons are also made to work across the range, not just the current TITAN Evo but chairs the company sold years ago. The effect is a hedge against planned obsolescence: instead of a fresh $600 USD purchase every few years, the chair under you keeps getting incrementally better.The cultural fluency, it turns out, comes from the same people who obsess over foam. Choo grew up on Batman and anime, and when I asked what separates a good collaboration from a cynical one, the answer was about understanding an IP well enough to honor it. You see it in the details: the Venom-black tendrils creeping up the Spider-Man chair, the hand-drawn Pokémon with no two poses alike, the carbon fiber the designers fought to include on the Automobili Lamborghini edition because the material is Lamborghini. None of that lands by accident: the designers pour real time into each collaboration, researching a franchise until they understand which details actually carry its identity, the ins and outs an outsider would miss. It's Choo's point in practice: honoring an IP starts with understanding it.The proof is in where the chairs ended up. The McLaren Technology Centre is furnished with their McLaren-themed chairs. The Dark Knight Edition, their first Special Edition release, is the one Zimmer bought for his studio — and recommended to his fellow composers. The character caught his eye, but the consistent support is what kept it there while he spent hours creating some of the best musical scores in history. Jim Lee even drew Bruce Wayne sitting in one in Batman #159 (Volume 3). View this post on Instagram A post shared by Jim Lee (@jimlee)A composer, a chess grandmaster, a footballer, a day-trader turned folk hero: lives that look nothing alike, joined by long, concentrated hours in a seated position, and by a chair that never makes them choose between working and unwinding in it. It's less that Secretlab chased the culture and more that it built the one thing all of them needed. And they keep tuning it, variation after variation, in changes small enough that most owners will never know were made but will feel every time they sit down.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Supreme and Dickies Reunite for an Extensive Fall 2026 Collection
Entertainment.text: SummarySupreme and Dickies have officially unveiled a new collaborative apparel collection designed for the Fall 2026 seasonThe extensive lineup includes durable workwear essentials like leather hooded work jackets and flannel-lined double knee painter pantsThe highly anticipated collection releases globally on November 19 with a subsequent launch in Asia on November 21Supreme and Dickies have reunited to officially unveil their new collaborative Fall 2026 Collection. Merging the New York streetwear institution's bold aesthetic with the heritage workwear brand's longstanding commitment to rugged durability, the upcoming release delivers a robust selection of heavy-duty cold-weather staples and completely reimagined apparel classics.Leading the Fall 2026 assortment is a range of premium outerwear engineered to combat the dropping temperatures. The collection is highlighted by the Supreme x Dickies Leather Hooded Work Jacket, which elevates a traditional utilitarian silhouette, alongside the heavy-duty Flannel Lined Hooded Work Jacket. For versatile layering options, the extensive lineup also features a Quilted Lined Hooded Flannel Zip Up Shirt and a Quilted Zip Up Hooded Sweatshirt, ensuring substantial warmth and functional wearability throughout the harsher months.Rounding out the apparel selection, the collaboration introduces a co-branded Thermal top designed for foundational layering. The collection also reimagines classic legwear with the highly durable Flannel Lined Double Knee Painter Pant, merging heavy-duty construction with modern streetwear sensibility. To seamlessly complete the seasonal offering, the duo has produced a collaborative Script Beanie. The entire capsule perfectly blends dependable utility with distinct co-branding elements, celebrating the enduring legacy of both brands while outfitting the modern wardrobe.The Supreme x Dickies Fall 2026 releases on November 19, via the official Supreme webstore and flagship locations, with an Asia release following shortly after on November 21.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: WILDSIDE Yohji Yamamoto and moseyec Pack Their First Collaboration in a Custom Spray Can
Entertainment.text: SummaryWILDSIDE Yohji Yamamoto and moseyec collaborate on an all-black SHIFT FRAME GLASS.The release officially reveals Japanese rapper Vingo as moseyec’s founder.Each customizable pair is packaged in a unique spray can.WILDSIDE Yohji Yamamoto and Tokyo-based eyewear brand moseyec are taking on the SHIFT FRAME GLASS for their first-ever collaboration. The collaboration arrives alongside a major announcement for moseyec, which has officially unveiled Japanese rapper Vingo as the creative mastermind behind its operations.Centering around moseyec’s signature “SHIFT FRAME GLASS”, and channeling Yohji Yamamoto’s signature design language, every single component of the collaborative eyewear has been painted to ensure an all-black palette. The frames feature a unique structural design that allows the wearer to detach the temples and swap out components for different visual expressions. Each pair is equipped with UV400 lenses, offering 99.9% UV protection.Beyond the frames themselves, the premium presentation also extends to the packaging. Instead of the traditional luxury eyewear boxes, the sunglasses are housed in a custom spray can-shaped case. The canister not only serves as protection for the shades, but also operates as a nod to Vingo’s roots in street culture and the urban landscape of Tokyo. The limited-edition kit is rounded out by a co-branded cleaning cloth and box.The WILDSIDE Yohji Yamamoto x moseyec SHIFT FRAME GLASS is available for ¥44,000 JPY (approx. $400 USD), and will first release in Japan on November 20 at WILDSIDE Yohji Yamamoto Shibuya Parco. It'll become available online soon after, via WILDSIDE’s website and select physical locations on November 21.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Nike and One Block Down Elevate an Icon With the Air Max 95 Lux “Italy”
Entertainment.text: SummaryOne Block Down and Nike unveil the Air Max 95 LUX "Italy" and matching apparel.The premium leather sneakers feature Black, Red, Green, and White colorways.Releases start November 13 at OBD, with a November 19 global launch.One Block Down and Nike have officially unveiled their latest collaboration: the Air Max 95 LUX “Italy”, alongside a football-inspired apparel capsule. Centered on the rich cultural intersections of Italian footwear craftsmanship and the 1990s golden era of Nike Football, the collaboration serves as a contemporary evolution of the original Made-in-Italy Air Max 95 LUX from 2001.Rather than reproducing the original 2001 model, One Block Down opted to elevate the silhouette by introducing a newly sculpted, padded upper that honors the original sneaker while feeling contemporary. Constructed with premium Italian leather chosen for its distinct character, the footwear is available in four distinct colorways: a Black edition pays tribute to the original 2001 release, while Red, White, and Green editions serve as a nod to the Italian tricolor. The latter three feature digitally printed gradients that were developed and applied directly in Italy.Accompanying the sneakers is a technical apparel capsule collection inspired by Nike Football’s heritage. The collection includes a jersey, jacket, trousers, and two skull caps that reinterpret the iconic Nike Football Dorito identity and Total 90 branding rather than simply reproducing them. As a nod to One Block Down’s founding year and its ethos to “give everything from day one,” the Total 90 symbol is flipped to read “09”. Additional tributes to the Italian flag are woven throughout the garments’ construction, highlighted by the contrast stitching on all garments and an internal tricolor tape featured on the Training T-shirt.The One Block Down x Nike Air Max 95 LUX “Italy” collection launches on November 13. The Black colorway and accompanying apparel capsule collection will drop both online on One Block Down’s website and in-store at One Block Down’s Milan flagship, while the Red, Green, and White colorways will be available exclusively in-store. A wider global release for the Black colorway will follow on November 19 through Nike’s website and select retailers.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: The Nike Dunk Low “Grandma’s Couch” Brings Vintage Living-Room Charm to the Court Classic
Entertainment.text: Name: Nike Dunk Low Retro Premium “Grandma’s Couch”Colorway: Golden Hops/Velvet BrownSKU: JF4566-900MSRP: $130 USDRelease Date: Available NowWhere to Buy: NikeNike brings a heavy dose of nostalgia to its latest release with the Dunk Low Retro Premium “Grandma’s Couch,” officially arriving in a “Golden Hops/Velvet Brown” colorway. True to its playful nickname, the sneaker’s entire upper is wrapped in a rich, textured velvet fabric decorated with an elaborate, vintage-inspired floral brocade pattern. The deep autumnal palette of golden hues and velvety browns evokes the comforting, familiar aesthetic of classic living room upholstery. This heavily patterned execution transforms the traditional basketball silhouette into a highly tactile, lifestyle-focused statement piece perfect for the fall and winter seasons.Contrasting the busy floral upper, the design incorporates carefully considered branding and structural embellishments. The iconic Nike Swooshes on both the medial and lateral sides are uniquely rendered using puffy white stitching, outlined by subtle brown piping that gives the logos a distinct, three-dimensional definition. To balance the warm tones, a muted "Pale Ivory" canvas tongue is matched by complementary laces and a premium leather inner lining. Finished with a classic rubber sole unit, the "Grandma's Couch" Dunk Low merges heritage athletic DNA with a cozy, granny-chic aesthetic.Set your reminders and get ahead of what’s dropping next on Hypebeast Drops.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Margot Robbie Set to Star in A24's 'The Week of Pain'
Entertainment.text: SummaryMargot Robbie will star in the upcoming film 'The Week of Pain' directed by Kristoffer BorgliA24 will finance and produce the project alongside Square Peg, Dilemma Films, and Robbie's LuckyChapThe announcement follows Borgli's recent box office success with The Drama starring Robert Pattinson and ZendayaA24 is teaming up with director Kristoffer Borgli and actress Margot Robbie for an upcoming feature film titled The Week of Pain. Set to be financed and produced by A24, the project will also feature production contributions from Ari Aster and Lars Knudsen’s Square Peg banner, alongside Dilemma Films and Robbie’s own LuckyChap production company.While official plot details for The Week of Pain remain heavily under wraps, the film is expected to deliver the squirmy, cringe-comedy drama that has become Borgli's signature following works like Dream Scenario and Sick of Myself. The new project reunites Square Peg and A24 with the filmmaker following their collaboration on April’s The Drama. That original dramedy, which starred Robert Pattinson and Zendaya, proved to be a massive box office success, grossing $135 million USD globally against a slim $28 million USD budget.For Robbie, the casting announcement follows her recent appearance in the Warner Bros. cinematic adaptation of the literary romance Wuthering Heights. Starring alongside Jacob Elordi as Heathcliff, the film rocketed to $241 million USD worldwide. Looking ahead, the superstar is also set to star alongside Bradley Cooper in a highly anticipated Ocean’s 11 prequel centered around an epic heist at the 1962 Monaco Grand Prix.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: G-SHOCK x XG Reunite for a Tattoo-Inspired Take on the Classic 6900
Entertainment.text: SummaryG-SHOCK reunites with X-POP group XG for the metal-bezel GM-6900XG-8 watch.Features a tattoo-printed translucent strap, hesonoo kanji caseback, and howling wolf backlight.Built with 200M water resistance, dropping November 2026 in custom collector's packaging.G-SHOCK has reunited with its global brand ambassador, the seven-member X-POP group XG, G-SHOCK has teamed up with its global brand ambassador XG for a second collaboration watch. The seven-member group, made up of JURIN, CHISA, HINATA, HARVEY, JURIA, MAYA and COCONA, has built its own “X-POP” sound that sits outside the usual J-POP and K-POP lines, a rebellious streak Casio ties to G-SHOCK’s “Never Give Up” ethos.The new GM-6900XG-8 is built around the creative concept “TIME, INKED ON YOU,” which treats the watch less as a tool for keeping time and more as something worn like ink on the wrist, carrying the feeling of XG’s music. It starts from the classic 6900 shape, adding a silvery metal bezel meant to evoke the weight of accumulated time, and a translucent band printed with the group’s full name, “Xtraordinary Genes,” in multi-angle print for a tattoo-like effect.Packed with custom details honoring the septet, the watch features an engraved "X" motif on its signature front button. Pressing the "X" button will light up the display, revealing a howling wolf, which is the fandom’s symbol. The caseback is engraved with the Japanese character "緒," the last character of hesonoo, the chant the members share in a circle before going on stage, standing for the bond between XG and ALPHAZ. Even the special packaging carries a hidden graphic of seven wolves on its base, one for each member.Under the styling, it’s a standard G-SHOCK: a resin and stainless steel case, complete with 200-meter water resistance, a 1/100-second stopwatch, countdown timer, multi-function alarm, flash alert, a Super Illuminator LED backlight and roughly five years of battery life.Casio lists the watch as a new release for this month, but an exact release date and regional availability have yet to be confirmed. For more details, keep an eye out on the official webpage for the collaboration via Casio. View this post on InstagramClick here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Buffer Plugs Into Sony’s Studio and Camcorder Legends for Its Latest Capsule
Entertainment.text: SummaryBuffer has made its own version of Sony’s MDR-CD900ST studio headphones, labeled the Buffer SPThree graphic T-shirts are based on Sony hardware, from a broadcast monitor to a 2000s camcorderEach T-shirt has a small chest graphic and a larger back print that tells a different sceneBuffer has released a Sony-inspired capsule led by the MDR-CD900ST Buffer SP, its version of the Japanese studio headphone, alongside three graphic T-shirts based on Sony gear. The release celebrates the tools behind making and listening to music and video, from the recording booth to the skate video.The MDR-CD900ST has long been a recording-studio standard for checking vocals and performances, and Buffer leaves the sound engineering untouched. The Buffer SP edition comes in black, with the Buffer logo and the line “Protecting you from the world friction” on the ear cup label. Specs follow the studio original: 63 Ω impedance, a 1,000 mW maximum input, a 5 to 30,000 Hz frequency response and a 2.5 m cable ending in a 6.3 mm stereo plug, with a 3.5 mm mini plug adapter included. The Sony headphones weigh about 200 g without the cable and are made in Japan, and they ship with a natural wood block.The PVM-6041Q T-shirt is based on stacking monitors to make video art. Its back shows a wall of nine screens playing weather-forecast and news-style images next to “Buffy” and “Buffer” lettering, while a single monitor showing Buffy sits small on the chest. Front and back look intentionally different, and the shirt comes in White and Black.The DCR-VX2000 T-shirt is the most personal of the three. The product copy says Buffy relied on this Sony camcorder more than any other while shooting independent films in the early 2000s. The left chest has a small skater holding a camera, and the back is covered with a large shot of the VX2000 framed by a filmer’s hands and feet. The VX2000 became one of the most iconic cameras in skate video during that era, so the reference will land with anyone who grew up on skate tapes. It comes in Black and Blue.The MDR-CD900ST T-shirt links the capsule back to the headphones. On the front, the headphones frame a row of alphabet blocks spelling “Buffer,” and the back shows a listener wearing them in profile, putting the tool and the person using it on one shirt. It comes in Green and White.The Buffer capsule drops November 21 via the Buffer Online Store, with a limit of two per product.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Brain Dead x adidas Originals Complete the Adventure Collection With Apparel and Accessories
Entertainment.text: SummaryBrain Dead and adidas Originals have revealed apparel and accessories for their latest collaboration.The capsule collection includes a shaggy half-zip fleece, lilac crewneck, crackle-print cargo pants and more.A fuzzy “DEAD” trapper beanie and carabiner-clipped socks round out the drop alongisde the previously revealed ZUPERKLIMB sneakers.Brain Dead and adidas Originals are rounding out their ZUPERKLIMB revival with a full apparel and accessories collection that brings back adidas’ 2000s Adventure line from head to toe. The early-2000s approach shoe returns in the label’s signature hairy suede, but the clothing does just as much to carry the outdoor theme.The standout is a half-zip fleece in a shaggy, long-pile knit, with an abstract mix of purple, brown and acid yellow broken up by an olive yoke, cuffs and hem. A garment-dyed lilac crewneck sweater takes a more vintage approach, with black Three Stripes down the sleeves and tonal embroidered logos on the chest. Dark grey nylon cargo pants have a crackled, all-over print, front pleats and a side cargo pocket with a co-branded patch. Product imagery also shows a brown tee with olive raglan sleeves, black stripes and red piping that the press release doesn’t mention. Each piece carries adidas’ Adventure logo, often alongside Brain Dead’s head motif.The accessories bring the shaggy texture back. A fuzzy trapper-style beanie in lilac and brown has ear flaps, long braided ties and a bright yellow band spelling “DEAD” across the front. Olive-and-brown terry crew socks pair the Adventure logo with the Brain Dead head, and come clipped together with a metallic carabiner carrying co-branded details. The collection reflects Brain Dead’s talent for bringing overlooked corners of the adidas archive back into focus. It follows the Samba Bowling packs earlier this year, and here the duo pushes that approach into technical climbing and hiking gear. The Brain Dead x adidas Originals Adventure collection releases in limited quantities on November 20 via CONFIRMED, select adidas stores and retailers and wearebraindead.com.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: SEGA Unveils Brutal “Act 2: Kure” Trailer for ‘Stranger Than Heaven’
Entertainment.text: SummarySEGA’s Stranger Than Heavendrops its “Act 2: Kure” story trailer.The prequel explores Makoto Daito’s 1929 yakuza rise in Hiroshima.The preview highlights brutal combat, sword clashes, and heavy emotional stakes.mineSEGA and Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio (RGG) have released the second story trailer for Stranger Than Heaven, moving Makoto Daito’s saga from Kokura in 1915 to Kure, Hiroshima, in 1929. The new footage opens with Daito trying to get close to Genzo Iwaki, the “Emperor of Kure,” and being surrounded by Iwaki’s guards before he is granted an audience. A key moment shows Daito accepting a ceremonial sake cup from Iwaki, sealing his entry into the yakuza after an attack on the family’s patriarch.From there, his new role takes shape: he oversees the city’s gambling halls and collects debts owed to the clan. The trailer intercuts his rise with combat as he earns the nickname “Red Oni.” SEGA’s official description frames the act bluntly: “In Kure, Daito swears his loyalty to Iwaki Genzo, and steels himself to commit any atrocities to climb the yakuza ranks.” The trailer also hints at the cost, showing Daito struggling with his life in the yakuza and facing the choices that led him there.Previously codenamed “Project Century,” Stranger Than Heaven is RGG Studio’s latest project after its long-running Yakuza/Like a Dragon series. The game follows Daito across five eras and five cities between 1915 and 1965. Its settings include Kokura, Fukuoka; Kure; Minami, Osaka; Atami, Shizuoka; and Kamurocho, the fictional Tokyo district that anchors the studio’s earlier games. The Act 2 trailer follows an earlier “Act 1: Kokura” story trailer, and SEGA has said more are on the way, each covering a different chapter of Daito’s life. Yū Shirota leads the cast as Daito, joined by Snoop Dogg as Orpheus and Tori Kelly as Suzy Day. Stranger Than Heaven launches January 15, 2027, on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X|S and PC via Steam and the Microsoft Store, and it will also be available on Game Pass.Read more at Hypebeast

Science & Technology.title: Can Robots Bring Stroke Surgery to Remote Hospitals?
Science & Technology.text: I am practicing brain surgery on a patient lying 6 meters away, out of my sight and reach. I press a foot pedal, activating the controller in my hand, and carefully steer a thin flexible tube called a catheter up through the patient’s blood vessels. I head for what I believe to be the brain, tracking my progress on the live X-ray feed. As I imagine finding a blood clot, David Bell, the surgeon seated to my right, helpfully reminds me that every minute a stroke goes untreated, millions of brain cells suffocate, swell, and die.The patient under the X-ray in Bell’s office is not flesh and blood, but a plastic container holding long branches of silicone tubing. The controller I hold comes from an Xbox. But the surgical robot is real. The Remedy N1 is designed for emergency operations, including thrombectomies, the standard brain operation for acute ischemic strokes caused by blood clots. Ischemia, a restriction of blood flow, is the most common cause of stroke.“We want it to feel a bit like a video game—a bit easy,” Bell says. “But we don’t want to dehumanize it as if there’s just another ‘game over.’ ” Bell, a clinician and former cardiac-surgery trainee from Australia, cofounded Remedy Robotics, based in San Francisco. With a team of engineers, he developed this robotic catheter and its related software to help ischemic stroke patients in remote and rural places, who lose crucial hours while being transferred away from hospitals incapable of providing care. According to 2025 data, at least 5 million people around the world suffer ischemic strokes every year. In the United States, stroke is the fourth leading cause of death. When Remedy Robotics cofounders Jake Sganga [left] and David Bell initially met, they matched each other’s energy right away.Christie Hemm KlokThe screen shows my catheter at a fork in the narrowing road, and I decide to take a sharp right; I think I can make it. This device feels easier to drive than a typical robotic instrument that I controlled on a hospital tour the summer prior. I say to Bell that here my movements are smoother, more precise—exactly the talking point you’d expect to hear from a surgical robotics company. Never mind that, Bell corrects me: “Smoothness and precision are not clinical outcomes. Neither is a surgeon’s ergonomics.” For Bell, the outcome that matters is whether the robot can get stroke treatment to patients who otherwise wouldn’t receive it in time. Today, only about 1 in 10 patients eligible for thrombectomy receive one.  That’s where the long-unrealized promise of telesurgery is meeting an urgent problem: providing access to thrombectomies before life-threatening damage takes hold. But can putting a robot in one hospital and a surgeon somewhere else actually close that gap? Remedy has already taken a first step, remotely testing its system on a small group of patients. “The remote stroke need is well known,” says Jake Sganga, who cofounded Remedy with Bell and leads the technology side. “It’s just a hard problem to take on.” Making telesurgery a practical part of stroke care will require more than a capable robot: It will depend on communications infrastructure, hospital resources and workflows, and ultimately, evidence that patients actually benefit.Why Telesurgery Starts With StrokeAs recently as the early ’90s, physicians who treated stroke struggled with “therapeutic nihilism.” A 1991 editorial by two lamenting neurologists expressed hope that a successful drug therapy for stroke would emerge that would “reverse the trend of nihilism.” Five years later, clot-busting drugs revolutionized stroke treatment, followed about a decade later by mechanical thrombectomy, in which a blood clot is physically removed from an artery.In a standard thrombectomy a surgeon snakes a flexible wire through a small opening in the patient’s groin. This guide wire sets the route for a fine hollow tube around it, the catheter, to travel through the blood vessels to the brain, where instruments remove the clot. Suddenly a stroke was no longer a sentence of profound disability or death but a treatable event.Yet decades later, thrombectomies remain inherently blind expeditions. The surgeon stands beside the patient, physically pushing these lines up, inch by inch. The only view comes from a live X-ray, which can’t see soft tissues like blood vessels. The surgeon shoots brief puffs of contrast dye through the catheter to illuminate the path ahead. A nimble operator can avoid scraping or piercing artery walls while bending the guide wire’s rounded tip around corners. But even these left or right turns are not intuitive. The guide wire can twist inside the body, and because the surgeon sees only a flat silhouette, steering it left may actually rotate the guidewire to the right. The N1 robot feeds the catheter along a rail lined with seven modules, using a thin wire that allows precise control through a patient’s vascular system, even from kilometers away.  Christie Hemm Klok If all goes as planned, the doctor reaches the brain and pushes instruments through the catheter to dislodge the clot, then carefully pulls everything back out. Bell remembers how thrombectomies felt when he performed them. “I’m one and a half meters away from my catheter tip. I’m not in control of it. I can’t see where the blood vessels are. I thought, what is the ideal way to do these procedures? It’s certainly not what I’m doing now.”Sganga and Bell want their robots to do two things: see what surgeons can’t see and be where surgeons can’t be. When I visited Remedy’s office in January, the team showed me their robotic arm and instruments that snap onto it. Motorized cartridges live on the robotic arm, one containing several actuators that use small gears to grip the threadlike instruments to move them in and out of a body. The instruments include a stent, an expandable wire-mesh tube used to pierce, grab, and yank a clot back out. It’s all typical stroke operation equipment—except for the catheter.Remedy’s catheter is steerable, so it doesn’t need a guide wire to pave its path. Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream. As I maneuver the catheter with the Xbox controller, Bell and Sganga tell me they made wayfinding a priority. Sganga toggles on a CT scan to overlay on the X-ray feed. Suddenly I see the bright three-dimensional routes of blood vessels along a path that had been invisible on X-ray.I noticed a pattern of small markings on the catheter. Sganga tells me they’re not for the surgeon, but for a computer-vision algorithm that tracks the catheter’s rotation inside the body. If an operator wants to steer right, Remedy’s software automatically translates that intention into the correct action. Instead of squinting at a 2D silhouette on an X-ray and mentally compensating for every twist in the catheter, the surgeon simply toggles to the right on the X-ray image, the Remedy system adjusts, and the catheter moves in the correct direction. This system grew out of ideas that Bell and Sganga were pursuing when they met at Stanford in 2019. Already a physician, Bell was completing an MBA and enrolled in a robotics class in hopes of meeting an engineer who might share his interest in creating a medical robot. The professor connected him to Sganga, a bioengineering doctoral student who was developing pathfinding algorithms for an FDA-approved robotic bronchoscope to navigate the lungs.Outside the body, a robotic arm advances the catheter while tiny wires tug its leading tip in any direction, as if an inquisitive worm is navigating the narrow branches of a bloodstream.Sganga’s engineering work had exposed him to surgical robotics companies that failed because they hadn’t chosen a valuable enough problem to solve. He sought a medical problem where a robot could prove its worth well before human trials, and stroke stood out. “It’s an already verified clinical need,” Sganga says, “Time.” When he and Bell met for coffee, they matched each other’s energy right away: “It was like ‘Hey how you doing?’ and then we were looking at medical images of blood vessels together off of his phone,” Sganga says.About a year after they both left Stanford, Bell and Sganga rented a two-car garage in Southern California and X-ray-proofed it with lead lining. “We called it the bunker because it had exposed lead on all sides, including the ceiling,” Sganga says. “It was just big enough to fit a bed and this rickety old C-arm [X-ray].” There they test-drove a prototype of their steerable catheter through silicone arteries—first controlling the robot on-site from another room, and then from a laptop hundreds of kilometers away. “We were trying to get an initial sign of life,” Sganga says. “And it was that moment that we realized that this could work.” Telesurgery’s Second ActDreams of remote surgery predate modern stroke care. In the 1980s and 1990s, the companies Computer Motion and Intuitive developed bedside robots to assist surgeons. Then, in 2001, French surgeon Jacques Marescaux and Canadian surgeon Michel Gagner removed a patient’s gallbladder from more than 6,000 km away. In New York City, Marescaux used a computer connected via high-speed fiber optics to control a Computer Motion robot in Strasbourg, France. The milestone, known as the Lindbergh Operation, was completed safely with no complications.But telesurgery did not take off after Lindbergh. Instead, companies invested in robots operated by surgeons in the same room. Computer Motion and Intuitive merged in 2003, more companies sprang up, and robotic surgery steadily entered the mainstream. Today thousands of surgical robots operate in hospitals around the country, assisting in roughly 22 percent of surgeries. In 2023 alone, more than 2 million surgeries were performed with da Vinci, Intuitive’s flagship platform.  Remedy mechanical engineer Chris Hapstack [left] and software engineer Campell Crowley adjust the N1 robot. Christie Hemm KlokIn the summer of 2025, telesurgery appeared to regain momentum when surgeons near Orlando, Fla., removed the prostate from a man 11,000 km away in Luanda, Angola. Around the same time, Intuitive demonstrated what it called “telecollaboration,” in which two surgeons on different continents operated together on a tissue model. Meanwhile, India-based SS Innovations has been testing cardiac telesurgery; in Panama, the Texas-based medical robotics company XCath has tested a steerable guide wire for thrombectomies. These companies are building on advances in computer vision and machine learning, yet remote robotics is hardly a sure bet.“The first procedures are going to be those procedures where time is critical,” says Brad Nelson, who develops surgical robots at ETH Zurich and is not affiliated with Remedy. Last year, Nelson coauthored a report in Science Robotics arguing that telesurgery’s future success hinges on finding emergency operations where patients can’t always reach specialists in time, including stroke, heart attack, and fetal operations.Surgeries that occur within blood vessels seem an attractive proving ground for teleoperation in emergencies. “If you have a hiccup, the nice thing about vascular procedures is nothing bad can happen other than the thing stops moving,” Nelson says. There’s neither a large open cavity to tend to, nor the urgent choreography one might need in organ transplants. If the surgeon loses connection to the robot while the catheter is inside a blood vessel, the operation can pause in place without damage.Nelson’s lab is also working on a stroke solution. He has partnered with the Mayo Clinic in Arizona to build microscopic robots—the size of a coffee grain—steered with magnets to dissolve a clot. When Surgery Depends on the NetworkAfter preliminary success in the garage, Sganga and Bell turned their focus to the environment where the Remedy N1 would live. Doctors and nurses advised them to improve the live audio-video feed, as any surgery is a coordinated team effort requiring constant communication. They were told to improve setup time, maintenance, cleaning, and began a series of conversations about secure communication and cybersecurity.  In 2021, CEO David Bell naps next to Remedy’s first X-ray machine in a lead-lined garage in Venice, Calif. Remedy RoboticsAbsent a cyberattack, the elephant in the room for any telesurgery hopeful is latency. Experts speak about latency, or lag, in terms of how many thousandths of a second it takes for a small packet of data to reach a destination then ping back to its original source. In a major city with strong 5G or fiber-optic internet, latency might measure in the tens of milliseconds. In rural areas, even in the United States, lag can drag above 100.Noticeable lag may not be a dealbreaker. When researchers in Japan analyzed five years of surgical simulations and demonstrations, they reported surgeons adapting to the connection speed. They paused. They moved more slowly. Remedy has noticed similar behavior in test runs. “We’ve actually found that operators are quite resilient to latency,” Sganga says.Still, Remedy targets a round-trip latency of no more than 150 milliseconds, below the average human reaction time of 200 milliseconds. Whenever latency sneaks above that threshold, the system pauses all surgical action. Bell and Sganga say they’ve tailored their system to work with the slower internet speeds common in rural areas that would benefit from better access to stroke care, claiming they recently operated their system from across the Pacific using a mobile hotspot. But sorting out the engineering details raises more questions about how telesurgery might change surgical practice. Bell told me he worries about what a telesurgical future could bring. What if surgeons’ skills erode? What if trainees become dependent on specific platforms? What if two patients need care from the same remote surgeon at the same time? “Is the person suffering a stroke in America necessarily more important than the person suffering a stroke in India? No,” Bell says. “So how do you figure that out? That’s something I think about a lot.”Where Telesurgery Could Work BestDuring a stroke, a blockage in the brain triggers symptoms within seconds or minutes. The following hour is the so-called golden period for saving the brain before the risk of permanent damage grows. “Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die,” says neurologist Archit Bhatt of Providence Medical Group in Portland, Oregon. “You really need to act fast.” Yet decades after the advent of thrombectomies, one in five Americans lives more than an hour from a hospital that offers the procedure.Medium and small hospitals often lack the 24-hour surgical team, experience, or equipment for thrombectomies, so they must transfer stroke patients to large hospitals. As a result, standard stroke care is concentrated in urban areas. For example, Alaska’s only two thrombectomy centers serving the 739,000 people who live or work in the state are both in Anchorage, leaving more than half of residents out of range.But the places most in need of telesurgery may also be the hardest places to deploy it. For starters, they may not have the high-quality network connections that remote surgery requires. Last June, experts from five major robotic corporations coauthored a list of technical standards for what they called “surgical-grade networks.” Mike Teodorescu, an information systems researcher with the University of Washington, says experts usually consider 100 milliseconds a safe threshold, but his team recently reported that many rural communities—and even most countries—struggle to meet it.  Neuroradiologist Hal Rice of the Australian Stroke Alliance remotely operates Remedy’s N1 System.Remedy RoboticsAnd connectivity is only part of the problem. The smallest and most remote hospitals may lack other support needed for thrombectomy, including neurologists, catheterization teams, CT scanners, and specialized intensive care units. “It’s an infrastructure problem,” Teodorescu says.Medium-size regional hospitals may be a better target. Although they rarely offer thrombectomies, many already have the right support, experience, and patient volume. “There is a window for a thrombectomy center in a reasonably sized town where there is a stable economy,” says neurologist Bhatt.“Every minute wasted or delayed, 2 million brain cells are going to die.”–neurologist Archit BhattTelesurgery could do more than bring a distant specialist into the operating room. Jasdeep Bahra, an emergency medicine physician and lecturer in Kilifi, Kenya, worries that telerobotics could concentrate expertise in cities—widening the skill gap between rich cities and poor towns. The thrombectomy access problem is real, Bahra says, but lower income communities might benefit more if a system like Remedy’s could both treat patients and help train clinicians on-site. Sganga says Bahra’s idea fits Remedy’s mission.“Digital operating rooms where you have surgeons that are over your shoulder as a mentor,” Bahra says. “If that’s what we’re talking about in telesurgery, that is the future for me.” Measures of SuccessIf smoothness and precision aren’t clinical outcomes, as Bell told me, what would count as success? One target is safety. In more than 1 percent of thrombectomy operations, surgeons unintentionally slice open a blood vessel, a feared and sometimes fatal occurrence that Bell believes robots can prevent.In September 2025, Bell flew to Toronto for Remedy’s first test in human patients. Ten patients had consented to nonemergency procedures with Remedy’s robot. A neurosurgeon with a laptop would operate on six patients in an adjoining room; two elsewhere in the hospital; and two at an entirely different hospital across town. The Remedy team had experimented for years on silicone models, like the one I test-drove. Tests on lab animals suggested that, compared with a human, their robot collided less often with blood vessels and finished procedures faster.  Neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira pilots the N1 system in 2024 for its first in-person robotic procedure, in Toronto. Remedy RoboticsIn the run-up to the Toronto procedures, the team measured internet latencies meticulously. Now they could only hope that their results would translate to human patients. “You’re never sure of how that leap is going to look, and it’s actually really hard to test,” Bell says. The night before the first operation, Bell barely slept.The procedures—recording images called angiograms from within patients’ blood vessels—were a success, and were completed nearly twice as quickly as the current standard. “I cannot explain the relief,” Bell says. Remedy considers speed one measure of success because it can allow doctors to treat more people.  In 2025, neurosurgeon Vitor Mendes Pereira and his team at Unity Health Toronto perform the first fully remote robotic neurointerventional procedures. Remedy RoboticsA few months after my visit, Remedy announced US $62 million in new funding to support upcoming clinical trials. A portion of that investment came from the University of California system, which will host the clinical studies within a year, according to Bell. Remedy’s first trials will be on-site elective procedures, such as treating unruptured aneurysms, before expanding to remote surgeries in Australia or within the University of California system, near the end of 2027.Sganga emphasizes that the on-site trials are not just a stepping stone. He’s come to believe that Remedy’s success depends on improving operations even when the surgeon is in the room. “The remote solution—it’s very flashy, it’s very obvious what that patient need is—but in order to get there, we believe you have to solve a meaningful problem on-premise,” he says. “Otherwise, doctors simply won’t use the system, and if they don’t use the system, they’re not going to gain the expertise required to operate remotely.”The steerable catheter and computer-vision algorithm are two features he claims will improve thrombectomies, remote or not. And as trials ramp up, Sganga says they will look at factors beyond safety and surgical speed. “How quickly are doctors picking up on this new technique? How smoothly are the bedside interactions going? How quickly are folks able to set up the draping and interact with the tools?” he says. Bell has wondered whether to add a photo or video of the patient’s face to the surgeon’s display to preserve the emotional stakes of surgery.These ambitions draw Bell and Sganga’s 25-person company into uncharted waters. Beyond one-time demonstrations, no robotics company has earned full regulatory approval for telesurgery, and no patient has been operated on remotely in the United States. Remedy hopes to change that. Decades after stroke research conquered the “therapeutic nihilism” that once defined the field, Remedy hopes telesurgery can bring thrombectomy to everyone who needs it, no matter where they might be.

Science & Technology.title: Advanced Metrology for Defect Detection, Tool Health, and Semiconductor Yield Enhancement
Science & Technology.text: In advanced semiconductor manufacturing, small defects can have a large effect on yield. Thin film deposition tools must stay stable and qualified. Process drift must be caught early. When a defect does appear, engineers need to know where it came from and how it affects device performance. This webinar shows how in-line inspection and offline characterization combine into one workflow, from tool monitoring to root-cause analysis.In the first half, Dr. Bitan Chakraborty from Intel, explains how surface scan metrology fits into station monitors for thin film tools. The session shows how baseline signatures and real-time monitoring reveal hardware wear, particle generation, and process drift before they reach production wafers. It then moves to in-line scans on patterned wafers. These scans expose layer-level defects and show how they form and spread through multi-layer device stacks. Linking this defect data to electrical test results helps teams find root causes and focus their yield improvement work.In the second half, Dr. Jacob Petersen from Evident Scientific, addresses a common question: what happens after an in-line tool flags a problem? In-line tools are fast, but they cannot always provide the details needed for a firm conclusion. Offline 3D optical profilometry fills that gap by combining three complementary inspection techniques in a single system. It delivers dimensional measurements and helps determine whether a defect lies within the sample or comes from foreign material. The session covers how several optical techniques support inspection from bare silicon to fully packaged chips. It also shows how automation enables fast measurement of features down to the sub-nanometer scale with minimal operator handling.What You Will Learn:How surface scan metrology in station monitors tracks tool health and supports the qualification of thin film deposition processesHow baseline signatures and real-time monitoring detect particle generation, hardware degradation, and process drift before production is affectedHow in-line scans on patterned wafers reveal layer-level defects and show how they propagate through multi-layer device structuresWhen offline 3D optical profilometry should follow in-line inspection, and how it measures dimensions and separates sample defects from foreign materialHow correlating tool health data, inspection results, and electrical performance links physical defects to yield loss and guides targeted improvement projectsRegister now for this free webinar!

Science & Technology.title: 28 Zero-Day Findings in Under Two Days. Is Robotics Security Keeping Pace?
Science & Technology.text: This article is brought to you by VicOne.VicOne identified an initial set of 28 zero-day findings in less than two days using AI-assisted research across software and tools supporting the Physical AI ecosystem. These include projects developed or maintained by Google, NVIDIA, and Meta, among others.Based on initial validation, all 28 findings are classified as zero-day vulnerabilities. The count may change following vendor and vulnerability-authority review, and some findings do not yet have CVE tracking numbers.Many of these tools help teams train, simulate, test, and operate robots. Weaknesses in them could influence the models teams build, the test results they trust, and the instructions sent to robots.These findings create two demands for robotics teams: responding as AI helps uncover weaknesses faster, and assessing how each one could affect robot safety and operations.What AI changes about vulnerability discoveryVulnerability discovery involves examining code, tracing how systems communicate, and testing whether a suspected weakness can actually be exploited. AI can accelerate parts of this work, helping researchers analyze more software in less time. Attackers could use similar capabilities.When the weakness is a zero-day — previously unknown and without an available fix — faster discovery can leave teams with little time to respond. While that exposure does not necessarily mean an attack has occurred, teams still need to determine whether they use the affected software and what an attacker could access or change.Where the findings sit across the robot lifecycleVicOne’s findings span three stages of the robotics lifecycle: development and training, simulation and validation, and deployment and runtime. Weaknesses at each stage could affect what a robot learns, how it is tested, and how it is controlled.  Figure 1. In this research set, 75% of findings involved development, training, simulation, or validation tools, highlighting risks that can arise before a robot is deployed.VicOneThe following scenarios show how a compromised component could influence the robot at each stage.Development and training: Hidden changes can reach the finished robotA team downloads a pretrained model to adapt for its robot. Loading a malicious file could give an attacker access to the training system, allowing changes to training data or the model itself. A manipulated model could behave normally during routine testing but respond incorrectly to a particular object, scene, or command after deployment. The risk can enter through a tool the team trusts, before anyone attacks the robot directly.Simulation and validation: A passing test could give false confidenceImporting a compromised scene or robot model could give an attacker access to the simulation environment. With sufficient control, the attacker could alter simulated sensor readings, physical conditions, or test results. A robot could then appear to pass tests that should have exposed unsafe behavior, leading the team to approve it for real-world use on the basis of misleading evidence.Deployment and runtime: Operators could lose visibility or controlAn attacker could exploit weaknesses to change files that influence motion planning or send malicious map data that crashes the operator’s monitoring display. Compromising a remote-operation computer could also put the instructions sent to the robot at risk. Depending on the system and its safeguards, these weaknesses could alter robot movement or leave operators unable to see what is happening and respond promptly.These are potential consequences and not demonstrated outcomes for every finding. Actual effects depend on the attacker’s access, the system’s design, and whether other safeguards prevent the changes from reaching physical behavior.In a separate demonstration, VicOne researchers provide a concrete example of a weakness affecting a protective function. The researchers exploited a vulnerability to prevent a robot’s remote-stop command from working. The case shows why teams need to test whether safeguards remain effective when the software supporting them is compromised.  Video 1. VicOne researchers demonstrate a vulnerability that prevents a robot’s remote-stop command from working. VicOne A published patch still needs to be proven safeAI can shorten the search for weaknesses, but a robotics team still needs to determine whether a fix is safe to deploy. Even after a software maintainer releases a patch, teams must identify affected systems, check compatibility, and verify that the update preserves intended behavior.An earlier successful test remains useful evidence. However, a newly discovered weakness may reveal conditions that test never examined.Three questions can help teams respond:Where do we use the affected software? Include training computers, simulation environments, and deployed robots.What could the weakness change? Assess whether it could affect models, test results, operator visibility, or robot behavior.How do we verify protection? Confirm that the fix addresses the weakness and that the updated system still operates as intended.When immediate updating is impractical, teams may need temporary safeguards, such as restricting access to an affected service, while a validated fix is prepared.From discovery to safer deploymentAs details from the 28 findings become available through coordinated disclosure, the next step is for robotics manufacturers is to connect each finding to its potential effect on development, deployment, and robot behavior.That work also requires understanding how threats could affect robot behavior and how to protect systems already in operation. VicOne Radeis helps teams identify potential zero-day vulnerabilities, assess AI model and system security, and use simulation to evaluate how these risks could affect robot behavior before deployment. VicOne Rthena supports threat detection and responses within approved policies during operation.  Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOneFaster vulnerability discovery matters when teams can turn findings into action: identify what needs attention, verify that safeguards still hold, and confirm that a fix does not introduce new risks. That is how cybersecurity strengthens robot safety as systems continue to change.For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper, “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

Longevity & Anti-Aging.text: Autophagy is a category of several different cell maintenance processes that converge on delivering broken or unwanted proteins and structures to a lysosome for disassembly and recycling. Confusingly, autophagy is also used as the common name for one of these processes, macroautophagy: a target is engulfed in an autophagosome, which then is transported to a lysosome and merges with it to deposit the cargo for recycling.
